summary: This document defines the XML patch document format, which expresses a sequence of patch operations to apply to an XML document, building on RFC 5261. It also registers the media type application/xml-patch+xml so these documents can be used, for example, in HTTP exchanges.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of resending a whole book to fix a few words, you send a list of changes. This RFC defines how to write that list for XML documents and what to call it on the Internet.

questions: how to patch an xml document over http
how do you send xml patches over http
subtitle: A format for sending incremental changes to XML documents over the network.

tldr.problem: When using HTTP PATCH to partially update XML documents, there was no standard way to express the changes as a structured patch document.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7351 defines a concrete XML document format with add, remove, and replace operations that build on the types and semantics from RFC 5261, plus a media type registration for use in HTTP.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now use application/xml-patch+xml as a standard media type for XML patch documents in HTTP exchanges, making incremental XML updates interoperable.

today: RFC 7351 is Informational. It has not been obsoleted and remains the standard way to format XML patch documents for use with HTTP PATCH and other protocols.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
The Hypertext Transfer Protocol has a PATCH method that lets clients send partial updates to resources instead of replacing the whole resource. Servers accept patch documents in standardized formats. For popular data formats like JSON and XML, the IETF publishes standard patch formats and media types.

RFC 5261 defined the types and semantics for XML patching: the operations (add, remove, replace) and how they work with XPath selectors. But RFC 5261 did not define a concrete document format or register a media type. This RFC fixes that by building on RFC 5261 and providing the missing pieces: a concrete XML schema, a complete document format, and the media type registration application/xml-patch+xml.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 5261 explained what patching meant but didn't say exactly how to write a patch document. This RFC fills that gap, providing the format and a label that servers recognize.

sections.title: Patch Operations and Structure
sections.content:
An XML patch document has a root patch element in the urn:ietf:rfc:7351 namespace. Inside it are zero or more operation elements: add, remove, and replace. Each operation has a sel attribute with an XPath expression that selects where to patch.

The add operation inserts elements or attributes at the selected location. The remove operation deletes the selected node. The replace operation changes the content of the selected node. Operations are applied sequentially: the result of one operation becomes the target for the next.

For example, <p:add sel="doc"><foo>New</foo></p:add> adds a <foo> element as a child of the document element. The operations reuse the semantics and detailed rules from RFC 5261, including how namespaces are handled and what happens with whitespace.
sections.plainLanguage: A patch is a list of operations: add something here, remove this, change that. Each operation uses a path expression (XPath) to say exactly where it applies.

sections.title: Complex Patching Scenarios
sections.content:
XML patching must handle several tricky cases. Whitespace treatment is configurable with optional ws attributes (trim leading and trailing whitespace, preserve it, etc.). Attributes can be added with a type attribute like type="@name". Namespace prefixes used in the patch must be declared in the patch document, and the implementation must carefully map those prefixes to the target document's namespaces.

RFC 7351 includes implementation hints in its appendices for handling namespace matching and patching. The specification points out that RFC 5261 had problematic interactions with XPath: XPath does not expose namespace declaration attributes, but the patch model needs them to decide if a namespace patch is allowed. These errata are incorporated into RFC 7351.
sections.plainLanguage: Patching XML is tricky because of namespaces and whitespace. The RFC explains the gotchas and how to handle them correctly.

sections.title: Putting It Together with Examples
sections.content:
A simple patch that adds an attribute to the document element looks like:

<p:patch xmlns:p="urn:ietf:rfc:7351"><p:add sel="*" type="@new-attr">value</p:add></p:patch>

A more complex patch might add a new child element, then remove another element, then replace text content. Each operation is applied in order to the same target document. The RFC also shows how to use namespace prefixes in the patch document so that operations work correctly with XML documents that use namespaces.

The examples in RFC 5261 Appendix A serve as examples for RFC 7351 patches; developers just need to wrap the operations in a patch element in the urn:ietf:rfc:7351 namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: Here's how you add, remove, and replace things in an XML file using this format. The RFC shows concrete examples you can follow.

sections.title: Using XML Patches in HTTP
sections.content:
The media type application/xml-patch+xml is now officially registered with IANA. When an HTTP client sends a PATCH request with an XML patch document, it sets the Content-Type header to application/xml-patch+xml. The server parses the patch document and applies the operations to the target resource.

The media type supports a charset parameter for character encoding (defaulting to UTF-8) and follows the same encoding rules as application/xml. The media type is intended for common use with any application that manipulates XML documents, making it possible to use the same patch format across different services.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send an XML patch over HTTP, you label it as application/xml-patch+xml so the server knows what to do with it.

viz.caption: Simple XML Patch Example (adding an element)

data.title: Add a new child element
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<p:patch xmlns:p="urn:ietf:rfc:7351">
    <p:add sel="doc">
        <foo id="ert4773">This is a new child</foo>
    </p:add>
</p:patch>
